title: Ships to scale
dek: Set the ships side by side to understand their size, roles and place in the war off Port Arthur.
intro: A longer ship is not necessarily a stronger one. In the Russian squadron at Port Arthur in early 1904, some cruisers were longer than certain battleships, although the battleships carried the heaviest guns and thickest side armour. The difference lay in what each ship was built to do: fight in the battle line, find the enemy, accompany torpedo boats or operate far from base.

The comparison places ship lengths on one scale. It opens with the Port Arthur squadron, and also shows four battleships from the Second Squadron, Varyag at Chemulpo and a selection of Japanese ships. The bars show hull length. The photographs show how the ships looked.

sections.title: For battle and reconnaissance
paragraphs: Battleships formed the heavy battle line. Side armour protected vital parts of the hull, while large turret guns were intended to engage enemy heavy warships. Five of Port Arthur’s battleships had 305 mm main guns; Peresvet and Pobeda had 254 mm guns. Even within one category, weapons, protection and machinery came in different combinations.

Cruisers needed speed and the ability to act independently: to reconnoitre, support light forces and attack enemy shipping. Bayan had a side armour belt. In protected cruisers, an internal armoured deck, sloping down towards the sides, covered the principal machinery. The word “cruiser” alone therefore tells us little about a ship’s protection.

sections.title: One war, different stations
paragraphs: At the outbreak of war, Port Arthur had seven battleships and the six cruisers shown here: Bayan, Askold, Pallada, Diana, Novik and Boyarin. Varyag was then at the Korean port of Chemulpo, now Incheon. The Vladivostok cruiser detachment was based farther away; its ships are not included in this comparison.

Destroyers, gunboats, minelayers and auxiliary vessels were also essential to the fleet. The destroyer Strashnyi tells the story of service in the light forces. Mikasa, Hatsuse and Yashima represent three ships of the Japanese battle line.

sections.title: When the squadron became the First
paragraphs: “First Pacific Squadron” is a convenient name for an account of the whole campaign, but in early 1904 it had no number. In his report on the first night attack, Stark was styled commander of the Pacific Squadron. Command powers and formation names changed during the war; “First” became established as the Second Squadron was prepared in the Baltic to reinforce the forces in the Far East. The familiar historical name should therefore not be mistaken for the precise designation used in January.

sections.title: The squadron that never reached Port Arthur
paragraphs: In autumn 1904 the Second Pacific Squadron sailed from the Baltic under Zinovy Rozhestvensky to reinforce the Russian fleet in the Far East. Port Arthur fell during the voyage, making Vladivostok the squadron's destination. Off Vietnam it was joined by Nikolai Nebogatov's detachment, which had left the Baltic later. The combined squadron met the Japanese fleet at Tsushima in May 1905.

Knyaz Suvorov, Imperator Aleksandr III, Borodino and Oryol were sister ships in the same division. Three sank at Tsushima. Oryol survived the battle, was captured on the second day and later served in the Japanese fleet. The comparison shows these four battleships of the First Division. They sailed alongside other classes of battleship, as well as cruisers, destroyers and support vessels.

sections.title: What the outline leaves out
paragraphs: The bars compare length overall. Books also give waterline length and length between perpendiculars, measured between different points. Substituting one for another can make a ship shorter on the scale without any rebuilding. The photographs show ships from different angles, so their size on screen is not a measure of length.

Length does not reveal coal reserves, machinery condition, crew training or damage. Even a shared calibre does not guarantee identical mountings and ammunition supply arrangements. Choose two ships of similar size and open their articles: compare how much hull space their machinery occupied, what the armour protected, and what weapons each ship actually took into a particular battle.

sections.title: Support vessels
paragraphs: This group includes vessels in the squadron and others that served it. Amur was built for mine warfare. Bureya and the steamer later named Angara carried cargo to Port Arthur. During the war Angara became a floating hospital. Mongolia accompanied the squadron as a Red Cross hospital ship.
